usage: add 선생님 when speaking to or about a doctor respectfully
받다 'receive' is the verb that pairs with 진료, not 하다
에서 marks the place where an action happens
examples: 저는 의사예요.
I am a doctor.
plain self-introduction; 예요 attaches after the vowel-final 의사
감기에 걸리면 의사한테 가요.
If you catch a cold, you go to the doctor.
한테 = casual 'to (a person)'; note 감기에 걸리다 'be caught by a cold'
할머니께서는 마을에서 오래 환자를 보신 의사세요.
Grandmother is a doctor who long looked after patients in the village.
환자를 보다 'see patients' is the idiom for a doctor practicing
nuance: 의사 is Sino-Korean 醫師 ('medicine' 醫 + 'master/teacher' 師), so the word literally frames a doctor as a master of medicine — which is why Koreans almost reflexively append 선생님 (의사 선생님) when addressing or referring to one, the way English keeps 'Doctor' as a title. Saying bare 의사 to or about a specific physician can sound flat or even slightly disrespectful, like calling them 'the doc'. Distinguish 의사 (the licensed physician) from 의자 'chair', which differs by a single vowel and trips up beginners constantly, and from 환자 'patient' and 간호사 'nurse', the other people in the room. The natural verb is 환자를 보다 ('see patients') or 진료를 보다/받다, never the English-style '의사를 하다'; a doctor 의사가 되다 ('becomes' a doctor), with the goal marked by 가, not 을.

Writing 의사를 되고 싶어요 with 를; the thing you become takes 가/이, so it must be 의사가 되고 싶어요.

usage: like doctors, nurses are addressed with 선생님 in clinics
the fixed verb is 놓다 'place', not 주다 'give'
에서 = location of the work activity
examples: 저는 간호사예요.
I am a nurse.
예요 follows the vowel ending of 간호사
간호사 선생님이 친절하게 안내해 주셨어요.
The nurse kindly showed me the way.
-아/어 주시다 adds the favor-plus-respect nuance
언니는 응급실에서 밤새 일하는 간호사예요.
My older sister is a nurse who works all night in the ER.
응급실 'emergency room'; 밤새 'all through the night'
nuance: 간호사 is 看護師 ('watch over' 看 + 'protect' 護 + 'master' 師) — the picture is someone who watches over and protects the sick, a warmer image than the English 'nurse'. The crucial register point is that today 간호사 is fully gender-neutral and is the only respectful current term; the older 간호원 (with 員 'staff member') now sounds dated and faintly demeaning, much like 'stewardess' in English, so avoid it. Don't confuse 간호사 with 간병인, the paid caregiver who attends a patient's daily needs (eating, washing) but holds no nursing license. Beginners also overuse 주다 for injections — the locked collocation is 주사를 놓다 ('place a shot'), and you 'receive' one with 주사를 맞다, literally 'get hit by a shot'. As with all jobs ending in a vowel, the copula is 예요 (간호사예요), and one 간호사가 된다, not 를 된다.

usage: 'summon' uses 부르다, the same verb as calling a person over
신고하다 takes 에 for the institution you report to
에게 marks the human you direct a question to
examples: 경찰이 왔어요.
The police came.
이 after the consonant ending of 경찰
길을 잃으면 경찰한테 물어보세요.
If you get lost, ask a police officer.
한테 = colloquial 'to (a person)'; -(으)면 'if'
사고가 나서 경찰관 두 명이 현장에 출동했어요.
Because there was an accident, two officers were dispatched to the scene.
-아/어서 'because'; 출동하다 'be dispatched' is the news-register word
nuance: 경찰 is 警察 ('warn/be alert' 警 + 'inspect/observe' 察) — literally 'to watch alertly', capturing policing as vigilant observation. The word is flexible: by context it can mean the police force as an institution ('경찰이 수사 중이다', the police are investigating) or a single officer on the street, so to single out one human being unambiguously Koreans prefer 경찰관 (官 'official'). Keep three look-alikes apart: 경찰 (police/officer), 경찰서 (the station building), and 경찰관 (one officer); beginners often say 'I went to the 경찰' when they mean 경찰서. Note the particle split — you 신고하다 (report) 경찰에 (to the institution), but you 물어보다 (ask) 경찰에게/한테 (to a person). Because 경찰 ends in a consonant, the copula is 이에요 (경찰이에요), not 예요.

usage: the activity is 요리를 하다; the person is 요리사
에서 marks the workplace where cooking happens
goal of becoming marked with 가
만들다 'make' is the everyday verb for preparing dishes
examples: 저는 요리사예요.
I am a cook.
예요 after the vowel-final 요리사
요리사가 만든 김치찌개가 정말 맛있어요.
The kimchi stew the cook made is really delicious.
만든 = past modifier of 만들다 describing the food
제 꿈은 호텔에서 일하는 셰프가 되는 거예요.
My dream is to become a chef working at a hotel.
-는 거예요 nominalizes the goal; note 셰프 for a high-end chef
nuance: 요리사 is 料理師 ('prepare/measure ingredients' 料 + 'arrange/manage' 理 + 'master' 師), so it frames cooking as the skilled craft of arranging ingredients. It refers to a professional who cooks for a living; the loanword 셰프 (chef) carries more prestige and a Western fine-dining flavor, while a traditional master cook may be called 조리사 (the term used on official culinary licenses) — overlapping but 조리사 sounds more institutional/cafeteria, 요리사 more general, 셰프 more upscale. The classic beginner slip is confusing the person 요리사 with the activity/dish 요리: '요리가 맛있어요' praises the food, '요리사가 친절해요' describes the person. Remember the activity is 요리를 하다 (do cooking), never '요리사를 하다'. Since the word ends in a vowel, it is 요리사예요, and one 요리사가 된다.

usage: the verb for singing is 부르다, the same as 'to call'
서다 'stand'; 에 marks where one stands
examples: 저는 가수예요.
I am a singer.
예요 after the vowel of 가수
저는 그 가수를 정말 좋아해요.
I really like that singer.
를 marks 가수 as the object of 좋아하다
동생은 데뷔를 준비하는 연습생이라 아직 가수는 아니에요.
My sibling is a trainee preparing to debut, so not yet a singer.
연습생 'trainee'; -(이)라 'being, since'; 데뷔 'debut'
nuance: 가수 is 歌手 ('song' 歌 + 'hand/skilled person' 手), a Sino-Korean pattern where 手 turns an art into the person who does it (compare 선수 'player', 가수 'singer'). It means a professional or recognized singer who performs for an audience; merely singing in the shower is 노래하다 or 노래를 부르다, and you would never call yourself a 가수 for that — claiming it implies you do it as a career, so Koreans distinguish a 가수 from a 연습생 (idol trainee not yet debuted) or someone who just '노래를 잘해요'. Note that the act of singing uses 부르다 ('노래를 부르다'), the very same verb as calling someone, which surprises learners. The object you like takes 를 (가수를 좋아해요), the goal you become takes 가 (가수가 되다), and after the vowel the copula is 예요 (가수예요).

usage: the craft is 연기 'acting'; 하다 pairs with it
나오다 'come out/appear'; 에 marks the work it appears in
goal of becoming marked with 가
examples: 저는 배우예요.
I am an actor.
예요 after the vowel-final 배우
그 배우는 연기를 정말 잘해요.
That actor acts really well.
연기를 잘하다 'be good at acting' is the set phrase
이 드라마에는 유명한 배우들이 많이 나와요.
Many famous actors appear in this drama.
나오다 'appear'; 들 pluralizes 배우
nuance: 배우 is 俳優 (both 俳 and 優 historically meant 'performer/entertainer'), an old Sino-Korean compound that already covers actors of any gender in film, TV drama, and theater — so there is no need to mark gender, and the English loan 액터 is essentially never used in normal speech. The thing an actor does is 연기 'acting' (연기를 하다 / 연기를 잘하다), not '배우를 하다'; that 연기 vs 배우 split (craft vs person) mirrors 요리 vs 요리사 and trips learners up. Distinguish 배우 from 가수 'singer', 개그맨/코미디언 'comedian', and the broader 연예인 'celebrity/entertainer', which includes all of them. The verb 나오다 ('come out') is the idiomatic way to say an actor 'appears in' a film or show. After the vowel, the copula is 배우예요, and one 배우가 된다.

Confusing 배우 (actor) with the wider 연예인 (any entertainer/celebrity), which also includes singers and comedians.

usage: the activity 운동 takes 하다; the pro is 운동선수
attach the sport name + 선수 for a specialist
따다 'pick/win' is the verb for earning a medal
goal of becoming marked with 가
examples: 저는 운동선수예요.
I am an athlete.
예요 after the vowel of 운동선수
그 선수가 마지막에 골을 넣어서 이겼어요.
That player scored at the end, so they won.
골을 넣다 'put in a goal' = to score; -아/어서 'so'
형은 국가대표 야구 선수라서 훈련이 정말 많아요.
My brother is a national-team baseball player, so he has a lot of training.
국가대표 'national representative'; -(이)라서 'because (he) is'
nuance: 운동선수 combines 운동 (運動 'movement/exercise') with 선수 (選手, '選 select' + '手 skilled hand' = a 'selected, skilled performer'), so it specifically means a chosen, competitive athlete — not just anyone who works out. That is the key contrast: 운동하다 / 운동을 하다 is what ordinary people do at the gym, whereas a 운동선수 competes professionally, and using 운동선수 for a casual exerciser sounds wrong. For a particular sport, swap in the sport name plus 선수: 축구 선수 (soccer), 야구 선수 (baseball), 수영 선수 (swimming); the bare 선수 is fine once context is clear ('그 선수가 빨라요'). Idiomatic partners include 메달을 따다 (win a medal) and 골을 넣다 (score a goal). Since the word ends in a vowel it is 운동선수예요, and one 운동선수가 된다, the goal marked by 가.

usage: 에게 marks the person you consult
선임하다 is the formal verb for engaging counsel
goal of becoming marked with 가
사무실 'office'; the place a lawyer works
examples: 저는 변호사예요.
I am a lawyer.
예요 after the vowel of 변호사
문제가 생기면 변호사한테 물어보세요.
If a problem comes up, ask a lawyer.
한테 = casual 'to'; 생기다 'arise, come up'
이 사건은 변호사를 선임해서 정식으로 대응하기로 했어요.
We decided to formally respond to this case by retaining a lawyer.
선임하다 'retain'; -기로 하다 'decide to'
nuance: 변호사 is 辯護士 ('argue/plead' 辯 + 'defend/protect' 護 + 'professional/scholar' 士), literally 'one who pleads in defense' — the 護 'protect' element is why it feels like an advocate on your side. Crucially, keep the legal-profession trio straight, since they share the 士/事 family but are different jobs: 변호사 (lawyer who represents you), 판사 (判事, the judge who decides), and 검사 (檢事, the prosecutor who charges); beginners frequently swap 변호사 and 판사. Note the suffix difference too — 변호사 ends in 士 (a credentialed professional, like 회계사 accountant, 세무사 tax agent), whereas 판사/검사 end in 事. You consult one with 에게/한테 (변호사에게 상담하다) and formally engage one with 변호사를 선임하다. After the vowel the copula is 변호사예요, and one 변호사가 된다.

usage: 기사 'news article' takes 쓰다; don't confuse with 기자 the person
취재 is the journalist's fieldwork; 하다 pairs with it
examples: 저는 기자예요.
I am a reporter.
예요 after the vowel-final 기자
기자가 시장에게 날카로운 질문을 했어요.
The reporter asked the mayor a sharp question.
에게 marks 시장 as the person asked; 날카롭다 'sharp'
선배는 십 년째 정치부에서 일하는 베테랑 기자예요.
My senior is a veteran reporter who has worked the politics desk for ten years.
-째 'for/into (a period)'; 정치부 'politics desk'
nuance: 기자 is 記者 ('record/write down' 記 + 'person' 者), literally 'a person who records' — the 者 'person' suffix marks an agent (compare 학자 scholar, 독자 reader). It means a reporter/journalist who gathers and writes news; address one respectfully as 기자님. The pitfall is the near-homophone trap among 기자 (the reporter), 기사 (記事, the article they write — also 'driver' as in 택시 기사, a different word), and 작가 (作家, an author of books/scripts): you 기사를 쓰다 (write an article) but a 기자 is the human who does it, and a novelist is a 작가, not a 기자. Their core fieldwork verb is 취재하다 ('cover/gather news'), and they 인터뷰를 하다 (do interviews). Since 기자 ends in a vowel the copula is 기자예요, and questions to one take 에게/한테 (기자에게 질문하다).

mistakes: Confusing 기자 (the reporter) with 기사 (the article, or a driver); you write 기사를 쓰다, but the person is the 기자.

Saying 기자를 질문하다; you ask to someone, so it is 기자에게/한테 질문하다.

usage: 군대 'the army (as an institution/service)'; 에 marks it
복무하다 is the formal verb for doing service; 으로 'as'
군 복무 is the standard phrase for the mandatory term
examples: 저는 군인이에요.
I am a soldier.
이에요 after the consonant ending of 군인
사촌 형은 지금 군대에서 군인으로 복무하고 있어요.
My cousin is now serving as a soldier in the military.
군대에서 'in the army'; -고 있다 'be (currently) doing'
할아버지께서는 젊을 때 나라를 지킨 군인이셨어요.
Grandfather was a soldier who protected the country when he was young.
-(으)셨- past honorific; 지킨 past modifier of 지키다
nuance: 군인 is 軍人 ('army/military' 軍 + 'person' 人), the general word for any member of the armed forces. Distinguish three related terms learners blur: 군인 (a soldier, the person), 군대 (軍隊, the military as an institution or one's term of service — '군대에 가다' means to join up / do one's service), and 병사 (兵士, an enlisted rank specifically, more technical/military-register). In Korea, because of mandatory service, most young men 군대에 가다 and spend a stretch as a 군인, so '군 복무' (military service) is everyday vocabulary. The prototype verb is 나라를 지키다 ('protect the country'), and one serves 군인으로 복무하다 with the role-marking 으로. The critical grammar trap: 군인 ends in a consonant, so the copula is 이에요 (군인이에요) — never 군인예요.

usage: the activity is 농사 + 짓다, a fixed pair (literally 'build farming')
밭 'dry field'; 에서 marks where the work happens
시골 'rural area'; 에서 marks the place of living
examples: 저는 농부예요.
I am a farmer.
예요 after the vowel-final 농부
농부가 아침 일찍 밭에 나가서 일해요.
The farmer goes out to the field early in the morning and works.
나가다 'go out'; -아/어서 chains the actions
할아버지는 평생 시골에서 농사를 지으신 농부세요.
Grandfather is a farmer who farmed in the countryside his whole life.
농사를 짓다 'to farm'; -(으)시- adds respect
nuance: 농부 is 農夫 ('farming/agriculture' 農 + 'man/laborer' 夫), and that 夫 'man' element historically skews male, though in practice 농부 is used broadly today; a more neutral, modern alternative is 농민 (農民, 'farming people', common in news and policy) or the polite 농사꾼. The activity is 농사 ('farming'), joined by the irregular collocation 농사를 짓다 — literally 'to build/make farming', the same 짓다 used in 밥을 짓다 'cook rice' and 집을 짓다 'build a house'; never say '농부를 하다'. Keep the worker apart from the place and the work: 농부 (farmer) vs 농장 (the farm) vs 농사 (farming). Crops and livestock are 키우다 ('raise'). Since 농부 ends in a vowel, the copula is 농부예요.

Saying 농사를 하다; the locked verb is 농사를 짓다 (the same 짓다 as in 밥을 짓다).

usage: 머리 here = 'hair'; 자르다 'cut' is the everyday verb
파마 (from 'permanent') + 하다 for the styling service
goal of becoming marked with 가
examples: 저는 미용사예요.
I am a hairdresser.
예요 after the vowel of 미용사
미용사가 제 머리를 예쁘게 잘라 줬어요.
The hairdresser cut my hair nicely (for me).
-아/어 주다 marks the service done for you; 예쁘게 'prettily'
저 미용실 디자이너 선생님은 손님이 끊이지 않아요.
That salon's stylist never runs out of customers.
디자이너/선생님 are common in-salon address terms; 끊이지 않다 'never cease'
nuance: 미용사 is 美容師 ('beauty' 美 + 'appearance/looks' 容 + 'master' 師) — literally a 'master of beautifying one's appearance', so it can cover hair, and historically skin/nails, though everyday use centers on hair. Don't confuse the worker with the workplace: the 미용사 works in a 미용실 (or the trendier loanword 헤어숍), so '미용실에 가요' means going to the salon, not the person. In real salons, customers and staff often address stylists as 디자이너(님) or 선생님 rather than the clinical-sounding 미용사, which is more of a job-category label; 미용사 vs 이발사 also matters — 이발사 is specifically a (traditionally men's) barber at a 이발소. The core verbs are 머리를 자르다 (cut hair) and 파마를 하다 (get a perm). After the vowel the copula is 미용사예요, and one 미용사가 된다.
